extracted.intended_audience: students, journalists, media scholars, and general readers interested in sociology and media studies
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and analyze the components and dynamics of a deviancy amplification spiral as described in media and sociological literature — how labeling, media coverage, public reaction, and authority responses interact to escalate perceived deviance. Useful for diagnosing moral panics and related media phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling and shaming leading to marginalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Occurs in societies or social environments when certain attempts to eradicate slightly deviant or criminal behavior by labeling and shaming it in a way that ultimately serves to further marginalize the people viewed as deviant, and cause them to engage in further deviance, thus intensifying social disapproval and perpetuating the cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originated in Leslie T. Wilkins' work; the act of public labeling/shaming is the initiating mechanism that can push marginal groups toward more deviant behaviour rather than reducing it. Look for rhetoric that stigmatizes individuals/groups and policies that publicly single them out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overreaction and moral panic
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor initial deviation can intensify into significant deviance if it is met with overreaction and moral panic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stanley Cohen documented this process; identify disproportionate emotional or political responses to a relatively small or isolated event. Caveat in the article: moral panics do not always include a deviancy amplification spiral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media confirmation and 'tip of the iceberg' framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported cases of such deviance are often presented as the ones we know about, or the 'tip of the iceberg', with hidden or borderline examples reported and thereby 'confirming the pattern'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for reportage that treats isolated incidents as evidence of a widespread trend, and for selective reporting of borderline or marginal cases that create an appearance of prevalence. Example: Cohen's study of media responses to the Mods and Rockers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignoring non-sensational evidence/statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: The less sensational aspects of the spiraling story that would help the public keep a rational perspective (such as statistics showing that the behavior or event is actually less common or less harmful than generally believed) tend to be ignored by the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A diagnostic sign is absence of context or disconfirming data in coverage. Anti-pattern: headlines and stories that omit prevalence rates, trends over time, or authoritative statistics that contradict the panic narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public concern and readership-driven feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the public are motivated to keep informed on these events, leading to high readership for the stories, feeding the spiral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High audience engagement can incentivize continued coverage; track metrics like repeated high-profile stories, follow-ups, and amplification on social platforms as part of the spiral dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glamorization or normalization increasing deviant behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: The resulting publicity has the potential to increase the deviant behavior by glamorizing it, or by making it seem common or acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether coverage inadvertently models or normalizes the behaviour (e.g., sensational profiles, attention to perpetrators) in ways that could encourage imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law enforcement focus and resource diversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Public concern typically forces the police and the law enforcement system to focus more resources on dealing with the specific deviancy than it warrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators include disproportionate policing, targeted operations, or reallocation of resources toward the perceived problem despite weak evidence of scale — part of the institutional side of the amplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial and political pressure yielding harsher sanctions and legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges and magistrates then come under public pressure to deal out harsher sentences and politicians pass new laws to increase their popularity by giving the impression that they are dealing with the perceived threat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for swift policy changes, mandatory sentencing proposals, or public statements promising tough action that are responses to media-driven public concern; these responses further validate the panic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority-media-public feedback loop (spiral dynamics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses by those in authority tend to reinforce the public's fear, while the media continue to report police and other law enforcement activity, amplifying the spiral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This encapsulates the cyclic interaction among media coverage, public reaction, and institutional response — seek evidence of reciprocal reinforcement (e.g., media reporting on police crackdowns which then generate more public alarm and further coverage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviancy attenuation (opposite process)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative theory in which some large problems are seemingly attenuated through not accurately measuring them, leading to statistics which underestimate the problem, leading to fewer resources dedicated to them and reinforcing the belief of those in power that they are not a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented by Button and Tunley as a counterpoint (case: fraud); use this as a diagnostic contrast — look for underreporting, measurement choices, or institutional practices that minimize perceived prevalence rather than amplify it.
